heading: INT. FIELD POST OFFICE - A REQUISITIONED SCHOOLROOM - DAY

units.text: INT. FIELD POST OFFICE - A REQUISITIONED SCHOOLROOM - DAY
A schoolroom stripped for the war.
Desks pushed to the walls and stacked with canvas mail sacks.
A blackboard still carries a half-erased multiplication table.
Dust slants through high windows.
Somewhere beyond the walls, distant guns thump at the slow pace of a heart at rest.
PRIVATE ELIAS WEATHERBY-NDLOVU (40s, spectacles mended with wire, gray at the temples) sits at the teacher's desk with a pile of letters.
He sorts them into pigeonholes made from egg crates.
His hands are careful.
He does not hurry.
He picks up a letter.
Reads the name.
Pauses.
Puts it face-down at the edge of the desk.
He picks up the next.
Sorts it.
The next.
Sorts it.
Then he returns to the face-down letter.
Turns it over.
Turns it back.
Elias does not read it aloud.
Someone else's handwriting does, in his head.
"...and the pear tree has finally put out fruit. Tell Papa. Tell him I kept my word."
units.name: ELIAS

units.text: He sets the letter down.
Squares its edge against the desk.
He takes a pencil from behind his ear.
Flips the face-down letter once more.
On the back, in neat capitals, he writes a single word: RETURNED.
Then, after a moment, he erases it.
He gets up.
Walks to the blackboard.
Takes a rag.
Wipes the multiplication table away, row by row, until only the nines remain.
He stands there a moment, looking at them.
He sits again.
Takes the letter.
Places it, gently, in the highest pigeonhole, the one nobody can reach without a chair.
Elias looks at the highest pigeonhole.
Then at the egg crates.
Then at the door.
Not today.
units.name: ELIAS
